questions.question: When is $A+B$ defined for two matrices?
options: Only when both matrices are square.
When $A$ and $B$ have the same size.
Only when all entries are positive.
When $A$ has as many columns as $B$ has rows.

questions.question: What does matrix addition do to the entries?
options: It replaces each entry by its absolute value.

questions.question: Why can you not add a $2\times3$ matrix to a $3\times2$ matrix?
options: They have the same number of entries.
Their total numbers of entries differ.
Their entry positions do not match.

questions.question: What is the additive identity for matrices of a fixed size?
options: The matrix with all entries equal to $1$.
The zero matrix of that same size.
The identity matrix of any size.

questions.question: Which ordinary property of addition still holds for matrix addition?
options: Matrix addition is defined for any two matrices.
Matrix addition is the same as matrix product.
Matrix addition changes the size of the matrix.

Which sum is defined?
If $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\0&5\end{pmatrix}$, what is $A+0_{2\times2}$?

Why does matrix addition require matching sizes, while matrix product has a different compatibility rule?
options: Addition uses rows with columns, whereas product uses matching entries only.
There is no difference between the two rules.
Addition works entry by entry, whereas product combines rows with columns.
Addition is defined only for square matrices, whereas product is always defined.

questions.question: If $A+B=B+A$, what feature of matrix addition is being used?
If $(A+B)+C=A+(B+C)$, what feature of matrix addition is being used?

Can two matrices with the same number of entries always be added?
options: No, their row-column shapes must also match.
No, matrices can only be added when they are square.
Yes, equal number of entries is enough.

questions.question: Why does entrywise addition preserve the size of the matrix?
options: All columns are collapsed into one column.
Each output entry is formed at an existing matching position.
Adding matrices always creates one extra row.
The size becomes the product of the two sizes, in every case without exception.
